newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: China tightens grip on fuel smugglers, hits trade.
newsitem.headline: China tightens grip on fuel smugglers, hits trade.

text.p: China has tightened its grip on fuel smuggling, affecting Hong Kong's oil trade and causing congestion at some ports on the mainland's southern coast, industry sources said on Wednesday.
They said the anti-smuggling drive, apart from being a crackdown on crime, was also part of an effort to tighten security ahead of Hong Kong's handover to China at the end of June.
"Security has tightened very much since early last week, and there are more patrols at the southern ports," said a source at a major oil company in Hong Kong.
"We see an increase in efforts to crack down on smuggling and illegal immigrants. They want to stabilise the situation before the handover," he said.
"There have been checks before but they appeared to be more strict this time round with more spot checks on oil vessels," said a Chinese trader in Singapore.
"They now look more closely at import licences, bonded warehouse and all necessary documents," he said.
In the first quarter of 1997, some one million tonnes of diesel entered China illegally.
Officially China imported two million tonnes and the smuggling probably cost the Chinese government some $60 million in taxes, industry traders said.
They said smugglers evade taxes which could amount to $60 for every tonne of diesel they sneak into China.
Traders in Hong Kong said up to 60 smuggling vessels ply between China and Hong Kong in the guise of dowdy fishing vessels.
Cold storage boxes, water tanks and any other available spaces on board are carefully sealed to carry the "black gold' which brings high profits, the traders said.

Hong Kong officially exports close to 200,000 tonnes of deisel to China every month. But the Chinese crackdown has dulled oil trade in Hong Kong, and caused congestion at the ports of Xiamen and Fuzhou some traders said.
Some oil companies in Hong Kong are concerned that a continued strict Chinese crackdown would disrupt contractual deliveries and deter genuine buyers.
"We have not been able to secure the incremental spot sales and have just been able to export our routine term volume," said an official with a major oil company in Hong Kong.
Traders said the Chinese customs surveillance was particularly strict in Shenzhen, causing some smugglers to edge north towards Xiamen and Fuzhou to avoid customs checks.
This had aggravated congestion at these ports, where most contractual ships discharged their diesel, traders said.
"There is a queue of eight mid-range (MR) vessels waiting to discharge oil at Xiamen with one very large crude carrier waiting just outside Chinese waters," said an oil major.

Xiamen normally handles up to 60,000 tonnes per month or two MR size vessels, but China imported extra amounts of diesel in March and April with smuggling vessels adding to the traffic at the port, traders said.
Shipping brokers said ships moving into the region this week were likley to face delays of up to three days.
"Congestions may get worse next week," said one shipping broker.
-- Singapore newsroom (65-870-3082)
